interactions.label: A 3-year-old child who was previously walking independently now refuses to walk

params.question: A 3-year-old child who was previously walking independently now refuses to walk and has lost several words he used to say. What does this pattern most likely represent?

answers.text: Normal variation in milestone timing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Normal variation may cause a child to reach a milestone slightly late, but it never causes the loss of skills already acquired. Loss of existing abilities always warrants urgent evaluation.

answers.text: Global developmental delay presenting for the first time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Global developmental delay refers to failure to reach new milestones in two or more domains. This child had already acquired walking and speech, then lost them — that is regression, not delayed acquisition.

answers.text: Developmental regression requiring urgent evaluation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Loss of previously acquired skills — walking and speaking — is developmental regression, which may indicate a neurodegenerative disorder and always requires urgent investigation.

answers.text: Isolated motor delay due to cerebral palsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cerebral palsy causes motor impairment but does not typically cause loss of language skills. The combined loss of both motor and language abilities points to regression, not an isolated motor disorder.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinction: developmental delay means milestones are not yet reached, while developmental regression means milestones that were already achieved are lost. Regression always needs urgent evaluation.
Well done. Developmental regression — the loss of previously acquired milestones — is never normal and always warrants urgent evaluation for neurodegenerative conditions.

interactions.label: A paediatrician suspects global developmental delay in a 2-year-old. Which featu

params.question: A paediatrician suspects global developmental delay in a 2-year-old. Which feature of a Child Developmental Unit most benefits this child compared to separate specialist referrals?

answers.text: It uses Western-normed standardised tools for more accurate scoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In the Indian context, the preferred tool is the DASII (Developmental Assessment Scale for Indian Infants), normed on Indian children — not Western populations. The CDU's strength lies in its integrated approach, not in using foreign tools.

answers.text: Multiple specialists assess the child together, producing an integrated clinical picture in a single visit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The CDU brings physiotherapist, speech therapist, psychologist, and developmental paediatrician together so that no single professional's blind spot is left uncovered, and the family avoids months of scattered appointments.

answers.text: It provides immediate pharmacological treatment that individual specialists cannot prescribe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prescribing authority is not unique to the CDU. Its advantage is the integrated assessment model — combining multiple specialist observations into one coherent diagnostic and management plan during a single visit.

answers.text: Referral to a CDU is mandatory before any early-intervention therapy can begin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no such mandate. Children can receive early-intervention services through various pathways. The CDU's value is comprehensive, coordinated assessment — not gatekeeping access to therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key advantage of a CDU is integration — physiotherapist, speech therapist, psychologist, and developmental paediatrician all assessing the child together in a single visit, giving a complete clinical picture.
Exactly. The CDU's integrated model ensures the whole child is assessed by a complete team in one visit, leading to a more accurate diagnosis and a practical management plan for the family.

interactions.label: A child who appears dreamy, forgetful, and disorganised but is not disruptive in

params.question: A child who appears dreamy, forgetful, and disorganised but is not disruptive in class most likely fits which ADHD presentation?

answers.text: Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The hyperactive-impulsive presentation is characterised by a child who is always on the go, cannot stay seated, fidgets, talks excessively, and blurts out answers. This child's quiet, dreamy profile is the opposite pattern.

answers.text: Combined presentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The combined presentation requires criteria for both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity to be met. This child is not hyperactive or impulsive — the dreamy, non-disruptive profile points to pure inattention.

answers.text: Predominantly inattentive presentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The predominantly inattentive child is dreamy, forgetful, easily distracted, and disorganised — but not disruptive. This is the presentation most often missed, especially in girls, because it does not disturb the classroom.

answers.text: This pattern rules out ADHD, because hyperactivity is required for the diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hyperactivity is NOT required. DSM-5 recognises three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined. A child can have ADHD with inattention alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: The predominantly inattentive presentation — dreamy, forgetful, disorganised but not disruptive — is the form of ADHD most often missed, especially in girls. Hyperactivity is not required for the diagnosis.
Correct. The predominantly inattentive presentation is the most commonly missed form of ADHD because these children do not disrupt the classroom and are often dismissed as simply dreamy or careless.

interactions.label: According to the DSM-5, which combination of findings is required to diagnose au

params.question: According to the DSM-5, which combination of findings is required to diagnose autism spectrum disorder?

answers.text: Deficits in social communication alone, without any repetitive behaviours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Social communication deficits alone are not sufficient. DSM-5 requires impairment in BOTH social communication AND restricted/repetitive behaviours for an ASD diagnosis.

answers.text: Impairments across three separate domains: social skills, communication, and repetitive behaviours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: That was the older DSM-IV triad. DSM-5 merged social skills and communication into a single domain, recognising them as inseparable. ASD now requires two domains, not three.

answers.text: Deficits in both social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! DSM-5 defines ASD by two core domains — persistent deficits in social communication and interaction AND restricted or repetitive behaviours. Both must be present for diagnosis.

answers.text: A below-average IQ combined with any pattern of unusual social behaviour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intellectual disability is not a diagnostic criterion for ASD. Many individuals on the autism spectrum have average or above-average intelligence. The diagnosis rests on the two core domains, not on IQ.

overallFeedback.feedback: DSM-5 requires BOTH core domains for an ASD diagnosis: (1) persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, AND (2) restricted or repetitive behaviours. Neither alone is sufficient, and IQ is not a criterion.
Well done. DSM-5 defines ASD as the co-occurrence of deficits in social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviours — a two-domain model replacing the older three-domain triad.

interactions.label: A newborn is diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism on neonatal screening. To

params.question: A newborn is diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism on neonatal screening. To prevent developmental delay, when should thyroxine replacement ideally be started?

answers.text: When the child first shows signs of developmental delay, usually around 12 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting for clinical signs of delay means the window of peak brain development has already passed. By 12 months, irreversible neurological damage may have occurred.

answers.text: Within the first two weeks of life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Congenital hypothyroidism responds dramatically to thyroxine if started within the first two weeks of life, during the period of greatest neuroplasticity. This is why neonatal screening exists.

answers.text: After formal confirmation of intellectual disability at age 5 years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting until age 5 to confirm intellectual disability before treating defeats the entire purpose of neonatal screening. The goal is to treat BEFORE irreversible brain damage occurs.

answers.text: Only after a repeat thyroid function test at 6 months of age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying treatment until 6 months would miss the critical early window. Thyroxine must be started within the first two weeks of life for optimal neurodevelopmental outcomes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Congenital hypothyroidism responds dramatically to thyroxine if started within the first two weeks of life. Early intervention during peak neuroplasticity — the first 2–3 years — yields far better outcomes than delayed treatment.

Exactly right. Congenital hypothyroidism is a classic treatable cause — thyroxine within two weeks of birth can prevent intellectual disability entirely, illustrating why early intervention during peak neuroplasticity is a pillar of management.
